source_text: Ταῦτα οὖν ἅπαντα ἐννοοῦντες, καὶ μνημονεύοντες τῆς φωνῆς τῆς λεγούσης· Ἐνοικήσω ἐν αὐτοῖς, καὶ ἐμπεριπατήσω· καὶ πάλιν, Ὑμεῖς ναὸς Θεοῦ ἐστε, καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐνοικεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν, καὶ ἡμεῖς πρὸς ἐκείνους λέγωμεν, καὶ τὰ ἀναίσχυντα τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀποφράττωμεν στόματα, καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἡμετέροις ἀγαθοῖς εὐφραινώμεθα, καὶ τὸν σαρκωθέντα Θεὸν δοξάζωμεν ὑπὲρ τῆς τοσαύτης συγκαταβάσεως, καὶ κατὰ δύναμιν τὴν ἡμετέραν, ἀξίαν ἀποδῶμεν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν τιμὴν καὶ τὴν ἀμοιβήν· Θεῷ δὲ ἀμοιβὴ οὐδεμία παρ' ἡμῶν γένοιτ' ἂν, ἀλλ' ἢ μόνον ἡ σωτηρία ἡμῶν καὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων ψυχῶν, καὶ ἡ περὶ τὴν ἀρετὴν ἐπιμέλεια. ζʹ. Μὴ τοίνυν γενώμεθα ἀγνώμονες περὶ τὸν εὐεργέτην, ἀλλὰ τὰ κατὰ δύναμιν ἅπαντες ἅπαντα εἰσενέγκωμεν, πίστιν, ἐλπίδα, ἀγάπην, σωφροσύνην, ἐλεημοσύνην, φιλοξενίαν. Καὶ ὃ πρώην ὑμᾶς παρεκάλεσα, τοῦτο καὶ νῦν, καὶ ἀεὶ παρακαλῶν οὐ παύσομαι. Τί δὲ τοῦτό ἐστι; Μέλλοντες προσιέναι τῇ φρικτῇ καὶ θείᾳ ταύτῃ τραπέζῃ καὶ ἱερᾷ μυσταγωγίᾳ, μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου τοῦτο ποιεῖτε, μετὰ καθαροῦ συνειδότος, μετὰ νηστείας καὶ προσευχῆς, μὴ θορυβοῦντες, μηδὲ λακτίζοντες, μηδὲ ὠθοῦντες τοὺς πλησίον· ἐσχάτης γὰρ τοῦτο παρανοίας, καὶ καταφρονήσεως οὐ τῆς τυχούσης. Διὸ καὶ πολλὴν ἐπάγει τοῖς ταῦτα ποιοῦσι τὴν κόλασιν καὶ τὴν τιμωρίαν. Ἐννόησον, ὦ ἄνθρωπε, ποίας μέλλεις ἅπτεσθαι θυσίας, ποίᾳ προσέρχεσθαι τραπέζῃ· ἐνθυμήθητι καὶ ὅτι γῆ ὢν καὶ σποδὸς, αἷμα καὶ σῶμα Χριστοῦ μεταλαμβάνεις. Καὶ βασιλέως μὲν εἰς εὐωχίαν καλοῦντος ὑμᾶς, μετὰ φόβου ἀνακλίνεσθε, καὶ τῶν προκειμένων μετὰ αἰδοῦς καὶ ἡσυχίας μεταλαμβάνετε ἐδεσμάτων· τοῦ Θεοῦ δὲ καλοῦντος ἐπὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ τράπεζαν, καὶ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ προτιθέντος Υἱὸν, ἀγγελικῶν δυνάμεων παρισταμένων μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου, καὶ τῶν Χερουβὶμ κατακαλυπτόντων τὰ πρόσωπα, τῶν Σεραφὶμ κραζόντων τρόμῳ, Ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος Κύριος· σὺ κράζεις, εἰπέ μοι, καὶ θορυβῇ πρὸς τὴν πνευματικὴν ταύτην ἐστίασιν; Οὐκ οἶδας, ὅτι γαλήνης δεῖ γέμειν τὴν ψυχὴν κατ' ἐκεῖνον τὸν καιρόν; Εἰρήνης πολλῆς καὶ ἡσυχίας χρεία, οὐχὶ θορύβου καὶ θυμοῦ καὶ ταραχῆς· ταῦτα γὰρ ἀκάθαρτον ποιεῖ τὴν προσιοῦσαν ψυχήν. Τίς οὖν ἂν γένοιτο ἡμῖν συγγνώμη, εἰ μετὰ τοσαῦτα ἁμαρτήματα μηδὲ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς προσελεύσεως καθαρεύομεν τῶν ἀλόγων παθῶν ἐκείνων; Τί δὲ ὅλως ἀναγκαιότερον τῶν προκειμένων; ἢ τί ἡμᾶς θορυβεῖ, ἵνα σπουδάσωμεν, τοῦτο καταλιπόντες, ἐκεῖ τρέχειν; Μὴ, δέομαι καὶ ἀντιβολῶ, μὴ κινήσωμεν τὴν ὀργὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ καθ' ἑαυτῶν. Φάρμακόν ἐστι σωτήριον τῶν ἡμετέρων τραυμάτων τὸ προκείμενον, πλοῦτός ἐστιν ἀνελλιπὴς, βασιλείας οὐρανῶν πρόξενος. Φρίξωμεν τοίνυν προσιόντες, εὐχαριστήσωμεν, προσπέσωμεν, ἐξομολογούμενοι τὰ πταίσματα ἡμῶν, δακρύσωμεν τὰ οἰκεῖα πενθοῦντες κακὰ, ἐκτενεῖς εὐχὰς ἀποδῶμεν τῷ Θεῷ· καὶ οὕτω διακαθάραντες ἑαυτοὺς ἠρέμα, καὶ μετὰ τῆς προσηκούσης εὐταξίας, ὡς τῷ βασιλεῖ προσιόντες τῶν οὐρανῶν, οὕτω προσέλθωμεν· καὶ δεξάμενοι τὴν ἄμωμον καὶ ἁγίαν θυσίαν καταφιλήσω μεν, τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς περιπτυξώμεθα, διαθερμάνωμεν ἑαυτῶν τὴν διάνοιαν, ἵνα μὴ εἰς κρῖμα ἢ εἰς κατάκριμα συνερχώμεθα, ἀλλ' εἰς σωφροσύνην ψυχῆς, εἰς ἀγάπην, εἰς ἀρετὴν, καὶ καταλλαγὴν τὴν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, εἰς εἰρήνην βεβαίαν, καὶ μυρίων ἀγαθῶν ὑπόθεσιν, ἵνα καὶ ἑαυτοὺς ἁγιάσωμεν, καὶ τοὺς πλησίον οἰκοδομήσωμεν.
thought_title: Approach the Eucharist with fear and purity
orientation: Chrysostom is concluding his homily by exhorting the congregation to honor God for the Incarnation and to approach the Eucharist with reverence, not disorder.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, considering all these things, and remembering the voice that says: 'I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them'; and again, 'You are a temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you'; let us also say to those people, and let us stop the shameless mouths of the impious, and let us rejoice in our own good things, and let us glorify the incarnate God for such great condescension, and according to our ability let us render to him worthy honor and recompense; but no recompense from us could come to God, except only our salvation and the salvation of our souls, and the care for virtue. 7. Let us not then be ungrateful toward the benefactor, but let us all bring in all things according to our ability: faith, hope, love, self-control, almsgiving, hospitality. And what I urged you before, this also now, and always urging I will not cease. What then is this? When you are about to approach this fearful and divine table and the sacred mystery, do this with fear and trembling, with a pure conscience, with fasting and prayer, not making a disturbance, nor kicking, nor pushing your neighbors; for this is of extreme madness, and of contempt not ordinary. Therefore he also brings much punishment and vengeance upon those who do these things. Consider, O man, what sacrifice you are about to touch, what table you are approaching; reflect also that being earth and ashes, you partake of the blood and body of Christ. And if a king invites you to a feast, you recline with fear, and you partake of the dishes set before you with reverence and quiet; but when God invites you to his own table, and sets before you his own Son, while angelic powers stand by with fear and trembling, and the Cherubim cover their faces, and the Seraphim cry out with trembling, 'Holy, holy, holy Lord'; do you cry out, tell me, and make a disturbance at this spiritual feast? Do you not know that the soul must be full of calm at that time? There is need of much peace and quiet, not of disturbance and anger and confusion; for these things make the approaching soul unclean. What pardon then could there be for us, if after so many sins we do not even keep the time of approach pure from those irrational passions? And what is more necessary at all than the things set before us? Or what disturbs us, that we should be eager, leaving this behind, to run there? Do not, I beg and entreat, do not let us stir up the wrath of God against ourselves. The thing set before us is a saving medicine for our wounds, it is unfailing wealth, a procurer of the kingdom of heaven. Let us then shudder as we approach, let us give thanks, let us fall down, confessing our offenses, let us weep mourning our own evils, let us render fervent prayers to God; and thus having cleansed ourselves gently, and with fitting orderliness, as approaching the king of the heavens, so let us approach; and having received the blameless and holy sacrifice, let us kiss it, let us embrace it with our eyes, let us warm our understanding, so that we may not come together for judgment or for condemnation, but for self-control of soul, for love, for virtue, and reconciliation toward God, for firm peace, and a foundation of countless good things, so that we may both sanctify ourselves and edify our neighbors.

choices.why: Glossary term for God's self-lowering in the Incarnation; required rendering.
Glossary term for the Eucharist; required rendering.
Glossary term for the Eucharistic offering; required rendering.
Glossary term for the believer as God's dwelling; required rendering.

choices.english: for this is of extreme madness
choices.why: Keeps the genitive of quality and the strong force of 'extreme' rather than softening to 'great folly.'
The verb means to kiss affectionately; 'kiss it' preserves the physical reverence for the sacrifice.

bible_refs.note: Ὑμεῖς ναὸς Θεοῦ ἐστε, καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐνοικεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν

pass_b_english: So let us keep all these things in mind, and remember the voice that says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6:16), and again: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3:16). Let us speak these words against them, and stop up the shameless mouths of the ungodly. Let us rejoice in our own blessings, and glorify the incarnate God for such great condescension. And let us, as far as we are able, give back to Him the honor and the recompense that is worthy of Him. Yet no recompense from us could ever reach God except our salvation and the salvation of our souls, and our diligence in virtue.

Let us not, then, be ungrateful toward our Benefactor. Let us all bring everything we can: faith, hope, love, self-control, almsgiving, hospitality. And what I urged you before, I urge now as well, and I will never stop urging. What is it? When you are about to approach this awesome and divine table and this sacred mystery, do it with fear and trembling, with a pure conscience, with fasting and prayer—not making a commotion, not kicking, not shoving your neighbors. For this is of extreme madness and no ordinary contempt. That is why it brings great punishment and retribution on those who do such things.

Consider, O man, what sacrifice you are about to touch, what table you are about to approach. Remember that you are earth and ashes, and you are partaking of the body and blood of Christ. If a king invited you to a feast, you would recline with fear, and you would take the food set before you with reverence and quiet. But when God invites you to His own table and sets before you His own Son, when the angelic powers stand by with fear and trembling, when the cherubim cover their faces and the seraphim cry out with trembling, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord” (Isaiah 6:3)—tell me, do you shout and make a commotion at this spiritual banquet? Do you not know that your soul must be full of calm at that moment? There is need of great peace and quiet, not of commotion and anger and disturbance. For these things make the soul that approaches unclean.

What pardon could there be for us, if after so many sins we do not even keep the time of our approach pure from those irrational passions? What is more necessary than what is set before us? What disturbs us so much that we rush off, leaving this behind, to run after that? No—I beg and entreat you—let us not stir up the wrath of God against ourselves. What is set before us is a saving medicine for our wounds; it is unfailing wealth; it procures the kingdom of heaven. Let us tremble as we approach, let us give thanks, let us fall down, confessing our offenses. Let us weep, mourning our own evils. Let us offer fervent prayers to God. And so, having cleansed ourselves quietly and with proper order, let us approach as those who come before the King of heaven. And when we have received the blameless and holy sacrifice, let us kiss it, let us embrace it with our eyes, let us warm our understanding—so that we do not come together for judgment or condemnation, but for sobriety of soul, for love, for virtue, for reconciliation with God, for firm peace, and for the foundation of countless blessings, so that we may both sanctify ourselves and build up our neighbors.

last_rejected.quote: What is more necessary than what is set before us?
last_rejected.source_quote: Τί δὲ ὅλως ἀναγκαιότερον τῶν προκειμένων;
last_rejected.why: Source asks 'what is more necessary than the things set before us?' — the English omits 'than the things set before us'.
last_rejected.fix: What is more necessary than the things set before us?
last_rejected.ruling: English 'what is set before us' = Greek τῶν προκειμένων; 'the things' is implied, not omitted.

last_rejected.quote: I will dwell in them and walk among them" (2 Corinthians 6:16)
last_rejected.why: The citation is to 2 Cor 6:16, but the Greek quotes Leviticus 26:12 (also cited at 2 Cor 6:16). However, the source text does not specify the reference; the translator added it. The source gives no book citation, and while 2 Cor 6:16 does quote Lev 26:12, the source itself does not identify the speaker as Paul here—Chrysostom presents it as 'the voice that says.' The added parenthetical (2 Corinthians 6:16) imposes a Pauline frame the source doesn't explicitly give, though this is arguable. More critically: the source has no verse reference at all, and the English adds one that may mislead about Chrysostom's immediate sourcing.
last_rejected.fix: Remove the parenthetical reference, or use 'Leviticus 26:12 / 2 Corinthians 6:16' if citation is required.
last_rejected.ruling: Ἐνοικήσω ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ ἐμπεριπατήσω matches 2 Cor 6:16 exactly; adding the reference is standard and not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord" (Isaiah 6:3)
last_rejected.why: The English cites Isaiah 6:3, but the source quotes the Trisagion as sung in liturgy, which matches Revelation 4:8 (Ἅγιος ἅγιος ἅγιος Κύριος ὁ Θεός) more exactly than Isaiah 6:3 (LXX has Ἅγιος ἅγιος ἅγιος Κύριος σαβαώθ). The source lacks any citation; adding Isaiah 6:3 is misleading since Chrysostom's form follows the liturgical/Revelation wording with 'Kyrios' not 'Sabaoth.'
last_rejected.fix: Remove the parenthetical reference, or note 'Revelation 4:8; cf. Isaiah 6:3' if citation is required.
last_rejected.ruling: Ἅγιος ἅγιος ἅγιος Κύριος is the standard Trisagion; Isaiah 6:3 is the recognized source. Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: our salvation and the salvation of our souls
last_rejected.source_quote: ἡ σωτηρία ἡμῶν καὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων ψυχῶν
last_rejected.why: The English adds 'the salvation of our souls' as if two things, but the Greek is 'our salvation and [the salvation] of our souls'—i.e., 'our salvation and that of our souls,' a hendiadys for 'the salvation of ourselves and our souls.' The English 'our salvation and the salvation of our souls' makes it sound like two distinct salvations rather than one salvation belonging to us and our souls.
last_rejected.fix: our salvation, that is, the salvation of our souls
last_rejected.ruling: ἡ σωτηρία ἡμῶν καὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων ψυχῶν naturally reads as salvation of us and our souls; English rendering is acceptable.

last_rejected.why: In this context, σωφροσύνη means 'self-control' or 'chastity'/'temperance,' not 'sobriety' in the modern sense of abstinence from alcohol. The English 'sobriety' is misleading; earlier in the same paragraph the translator rendered σωφροσύνη as 'self-control.' The inconsistency and the wrong sense here confuse the reader.
last_rejected.fix: self-control of soul, for love, for virtue
last_rejected.ruling: σωφροσύνη includes 'sobriety' in patristic usage; inconsistency with 'self-control' earlier is minor, not a major error.
